ABSTRACT: Herein, we report a photocatalytic regioselective 1,4-carbocarboxylation of 1,3-enynes with CO
2
enabled by a thiol-
mediated hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) and formate cooperative mechanism. This strategy uses formate and CO
2
as synergistic
carbon sources, to deliver a diverse array of aryl-, heteroaryl-, and alkyl-functionalized tetrasubstituted allene carboxylic acids. The
reaction exhibits broad substrate scope across electronically and sterically varied enynes and iodides, and facilitates late-stage
functionalization of bioactive molecules. Gram-scale synthesis and derivatization experiments further demonstrate its synthetic
utility.
A
llenes, characterized by their unique cumulated diene
system, are widely found in natural products and
bioactive molecules (Scheme 1a),
1
and represent highly
versatile building blocks in modern organic synthesis and
drug design. The radical-mediated approach has emerged as a
key strategy for allene synthesis, providing efficient, diverse,
and controllable routes to these structures. Its notable
advantages include facilitating multifunctionalization and
enabling the construction of complex molecular architectures.
2
Recent advances have established several effective methods for
generating allene intermediates, such as 1,4-additions to 1,3-
enynes,
2a,3
activation of propargylic derivatives via leaving
groups,
2a,b,3a,4
and HAT from preformed allenes
5
have been
effectively employed to generate allene intermediates (Scheme
1b). The resulting intermediates exhibit broad reactivity,
engaging with electrophiles, nucleophiles, and radical coupling
partners, thus providing efficient pathways to tetrasubstituted
allenes and significantly promoting the synthesis and
application of allene-derived compounds.
Among these, multifunctionalized tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoic acids are of particular interest due to their axially
chiral scaffolds and notable bioactivity, demonstrating
considerable potential in medicinal chemistry and functional
materials.
6
The carboxylic acid group not only enhances
bioavailability but also provides a versatile handle for further
derivatization, attracting broad attention from synthetic
chemists.
1a,7
Conventional synthetic routes to such com-
pounds typically involve the oxidation of allenols or hydrolysis
of allene nitriles and esters (Scheme 1c),
8
which often suffer
from drawbacks including multistep sequences and poor atom
economy. Earlier strategies relied on stoichiometric metal
reagents to generate allenyl metal intermediates, followed by
carboxylation with CO
2
.
9
Although transition-metal-catalyzed
carbonylative reactions using CO allow the introduction of
carboxylic acid groups, these methods require high-pressure
conditions and expensive metal catalysts.
6,10
More recently, electrocatalytic approaches have been
developed for the conversion of propargylic derivatives with
CO
2
into 2,3-allenoic acids under mild conditions.
4a,b
However, these methods are currently limited to the synthesis
of monofunctionalized products. Therefore, the efficient
construction of multifunctionalized tetrasubstituted allenoic
acids remains a significant and unresolved challenge in
synthetic chemistry.
Carbon dioxide, serving as a renewable and abundant C1
synthon, offers a direct route to high-value carboxylic acids in
alignment with green chemistry principles.
11
Nevertheless, its
high thermodynamic stability and kinetic inertness present

substantial challenges for catalytic carboxylation. In this
context, photocatalytic carboxylation has emerged as a
promising strategy for activating simple substrates, owing to
its operational simplicity, sustainability, and cost efficiency.
12
Of particular note is the photochemical generation of highly
reactive carbon dioxide radical anions (CO
2
•−
), which has
attracted considerable attention for driving efficient carbox-
ylation reactions under mild conditions.
13
Inspired by our group’s previous achievements in CO
2
functionalization,
14
we sought to develop a method for
synthesizing bifunctionalized tetrasubstituted allene carboxylic
acids via the regioselective 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes. To overcome the persistent challenge of competitive
radical 1,2-additions in such transformations,
2a,3a,15
we
designed a dual-role photocatalytic system. This approach
employs thiol as a HAT catalyst, along with formate acting
both as a precursor for CO
2
•−
radicals and an auxiliary carbon
source. By engaging a broad range of aryl, heteroaryl, and alkyl
iodides, this strategy enables highly selective access to diverse
difunctionalized tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoic acids.
To validate our hypothesis, we employed enyne 1 as the
model substrate to investigate the 1,4-carbocarboxylation of
1,3-enynes (Table 1). Systematic optimization of the reaction
conditions
revealed that employing Ir(ppy)
2
(dtbbpy)PF
6
as the photo-
catalyst, tert-butyl thiol as the hydrogen atom transfer (HAT)
catalyst, cesium carbonate as the base, and potassium formate
as the reductant afforded the target allene carboxylic acid 3 in
82% isolated yield with excellent chemoselectivity (entry 1; see
Supporting Information (SI) for detailed optimization). The
reaction did not proceed in the absence of blue light irradiation
(entry 2), other control experiments confirmed the necessity of
all components as omitting photocatalyst, thiol, formate, or
base abolished product generation (entry 3). Experiments
conducted under a N
2
atmosphere in the absence of CO
2
resulted in a significant decrease in product yield (Entry 4),
clearly demonstrating that gaseous CO
2
is an essential
component of the reaction. Increasing the equivalent amount
of formate had limited effect on yield improvement (see SI),
indicating that formate primarily functions as a reductant, with
only minor and inefficient contribution as a carbon source.
Substitution of Ir(ppy)
2
(dtbbpy)PF
6
with 4DPAIPN dimin-
ished the yield to 52% (entry 5), while other Ir-photocatalysts
exhibited lower efficiency (entry 6). Evaluation of alternative
HAT catalysts revealed reduced yields with DABCO (73%)
(entry 7). Comprehensive screening of alternative formates,
bases, and solvents uniformly resulted in diminished yields
(entries 8−10). Other radical precursors, namely both
bromobenzene and potassium benzotrifluoroborate, exhibited
markedly reduced reactivity compared to iodobenzene,
resulting in substantial recovery of starting material. (entries
11−12).
After carefully screening various reaction parameters, the
substrate scope of the 1,4-carbocarboxylation reaction
involving 1,3-enynes and iodides was systematically inves-
tigated under the optimized conditions (Scheme 2). Enyne
substrates bearing electron-donating (methoxy, tert-butyl),
neutral (phenyl), and electron- withdrawing (fluoro, chloro,
trifluoromethyl) groups all afforded the desired products in
moderate to good yields (B), with no significant difference in
reactivity observed (3-9). Both ortho- and meta-substituted
enynes provided comparable yields (10−12). Difluoro-
substituted, fused-ring and heterocyclic enynes were also
smoothly converted (13−15). Furthermore, the structure of
product 13 was unambiguously determined by X-ray
diffraction analysis (CCDC 2473796). In addition to tert-
butyl-substituted enynes, methyl-substituted enynes were also
compatible with this reaction, providing the desired product in
moderate yield (16). Furthermore, alkyl-substituted enynes
underwent analogous transformation to afford the target
product in 60% yield (17).

To further broaden the scope of this methodology, we
explored the applicability of iodides bearing diverse sub-
stituents and substitution patterns. Evaluation of the substrate
scope revealed excellent compatibility with aryl iodides
containing neutral (methyl, isopropyl, phenyl), electron-
donating (methoxy, phenoxy), and electron-withdrawing
(chloro, cyano, boronate ester, trifluoromethoxy, trifluoro-
methyl, ester) groups (18−28, 47%−80%). Nevertheless,
strongly electron-withdrawing substituents led to markedly
diminished reaction efficiency, as reflected in substantially
lower yields (24, 27). Aryl iodides with ortho or meta
substituents and disubstituted aryl iodides both maintained
good yields (29−31), indicating high tolerance to steric
hindrance. Fused-ring iodides (32), sulfur-containing hetero-
cyclic iodides (33), and nitrogen- containing heterocyclic
iodides (34) all afforded moderate yields, demonstrating good
heteroatom compatibility. In addition to aryl iodides, the
methodology was successfully extended to alkyl iodides, as
exemplified by the efficient conversion of secondary
iodocyclohexane (35), N-Boc-4-iodopiperidine (36), and
tertiaryiodoadamantane (37). In contrast, primary alkyl halides
exhibited limited reactivity under the current conditions. The
method exhibited excellent applicability for the late-stage
modification of complex molecules, as iodinated derivatives of
L- Menthol, Nerol, Empagliflozin intermediate, and Alectinib
intermediate all provided the target carboxylated products in
moderate yields (38−41), highlighting its utility for the late-
stage functionalization of bioactive molecules.
To evaluate the synthetic potential of this reaction, enyne 1
was subjected to gram-scale conditions (7 mmol), affording the
allene carboxylic acid product 3 in 79% isolated yield (1.69 g)
(Scheme 3a). Serving as a versatile synthetic building block
(Scheme 3b), 3 reacted with methoxy methylamine hydro-
chloride to furnish Weinreb amide 42 in 90% yield.
Subsequent treatment of 42 with methylmagnesium bromide
generated allenone 43. Silver nitrate- catalyzed cyclization of 3
proceeded to give furanone 44, featuring an all-carbon
quaternary center in 97% yield. Furthermore, 3 underwent
one-step esterification with TMSCHN
2
to deliver allenoate 45
in 99% yield, which was conveniently converted to allenol 46
via diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL-H) reduction.
To elucidate the reaction mechanism, 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpi-
peridin-1-oxyl (TEMPO) as a radical scavenger was introduced
into the standard reaction system (Scheme 4a). The reaction
was completely suppressed with 52% recovery of substrate 1,
and the TEMPO adduct was detected by HRMS, suggesting a
potential radical pathway. When the reaction was conducted
under N
2
atmosphere with added H
2
O, allene product 47 was
obtained in 46% isolated yield. Employing D
2
O afforded
deuterated product 48 in 52% yield with 96% deuterium
incorporation (Scheme 4b), directly confirming the existence
of an allene carbanion intermediate. To elucidate the carboxyl
source, H
13
COONa was employed as a tracer, and 22%
13
C
incorporation was observed at the carboxyl group of the
product, indicating that formate also serves as a carbon source
for carboxylation (Scheme 4c). Additionally, Stern−Volmer
quenching experiments (Scheme 4d) further demonstrated
that thiolate effectively quenches the excited state of the
photocatalyst.
Based on these results and literature evidence,
13a,m
a
plausible reaction mechanism is proposed (Scheme 4e).

PC*, which undergoes single-electron reduction quenching by

radical then activates formate via hydrogen atom transfer

reduction of iodide I by CO

2

Isomerization of V generates allene carbanion VI and

2

In summary, we have developed an efficient photocatalytic
1,4-carbocarboxylation of 1,3-enynes with CO
2
to construct
tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoic acids under mild conditions. Key
to this strategy is the synergistic combination of thiol HAT
catalysis and formate, which concurrently generates reactive
CO
2
•−
radicals. The method exhibits exceptional functional
group tolerance and substrate generality, accommodating
diverse (hetero)aryl and alkyl iodides, and enabling late-stage
modification of pharmaceuticals. This work establishes a
sustainable approach to valuable allene carboxylic acid
architectures using formate and CO
2
as synergistic carbon
sources.

reaction exhibits broad substrate scope across electronically and sterically varied enynes and iodides, and facilitates late-stage

utility.

Recent advances have established several efective methods for

Among these, multifunctionalized tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoic acids are of particular interest due to their axially
chiral scafolds and notable bioactivity, demonstrating
considerable potential in medicinal chemistry and functional
materials.<sup>6</sup> The carboxylic acid group not only enhances
bioavailability but also provides a versatile handle for further
derivatization, attracting broad attention from synthetic
chemists.<sup>1a,7</sup> Conventional synthetic routes to such com-

of allene nitriles and esters (Scheme 1c),<sup>8</sup> which often sufer

reagents to generate allenyl metal intermediates, followed by
carboxylation with

Although transition-metal-catalyzed
carbonylative reactions using CO allow the introduction of

More recently, electrocatalytic approaches have been
developed for the conversion of propargylic derivatives with

into 2,3-allenoic acids under mild conditions.<sup>4a,b</sup>
However, these methods are currently limited to the synthesis

Carbon dioxide, serving as a renewable and abundant C1

alignment with green chemistry principles.<sup>11</sup> Nevertheless, its
high thermodynamic stability and kinetic inertness present

To further broaden the scope of this methodology, we
explored the applicability of iodides bearing diverse sub-
stituents and substitution patterns. Evaluation of the substrate
scope revealed excellent compatibility with aryl iodides
containing neutral (methyl, isopropyl, phenyl), electron-
donating (methoxy, phenoxy), and electron-withdrawing
(chloro, cyano, boronate ester, trifluoromethoxy, trifluoro-
methyl, ester) groups (18−28, 47%−80%). Nevertheless,
strongly electron-withdrawing substituents led to markedly
diminished reaction eficiency, as reflected in substantially
lower yields (24, 27). Aryl iodides with ortho or meta
substituents and disubstituted aryl iodides both maintained
good yields (29−31), indicating high tolerance to steric
hindrance. Fused-ring iodides (32), sulfur-containing hetero-
cyclic iodides (33), and nitrogen- containing heterocyclic
iodides (34) all aforded moderate yields, demonstrating good
heteroatom compatibility. In addition to aryl iodides, the
methodology was successfully extended to alkyl iodides, as
exemplified by the eficient conversion of secondary

iodocyclohexane (35), N-Boc-4-iodopiperidine (36), and
tertiaryiodoadamantane (37). In contrast, primary alkyl halides

method exhibited excellent applicability for the late-stage
modification of complex molecules, as iodinated derivatives of
L- Menthol, Nerol, Empagliflozin intermediate, and Alectinib
intermediate all provided the target carboxylated products in
moderate yields (38−41), highlighting its utility for the late-
stage functionalization of bioactive molecules.
